q: How large is the gravitational force between two bodies of mass $1.0\,\text{kg}$ when their centres are $1.0\,\text{m}$ apart?
a: $F = \gamma \tfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}\,\tfrac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{kg}^2} \cdot \tfrac{1.0\,\text{kg} \cdot 1.0\,\text{kg}}{(1.0\,\text{m})^2} \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^{-11}\,\text{N}$. The numerical value of the gravitational constant is exactly the magnitude of this force in newtons, and the force is so small that it is not noticed in everyday life.

q: Why do a heavy and a light stone fall in a vacuum with the same acceleration, although a greater gravitational force acts on the heavier one?
a: The gravitational force $F = \gamma \tfrac{Mm}{R^2}$ is directly proportional to the mass $m$ of the stone, but the inertia of the stone also grows with its mass. The acceleration $a = \tfrac{F}{m} = \gamma \tfrac{M}{R^2} = g$ therefore does not depend on the mass of the stone.
